article.title: Why the Value of Information Depends on Whether It Can Change a Decision
article.why: 從 decision threshold 理解資訊何時值得取得。
article.author: OpenAI learning editor

sources.label: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy — Decision Theory

paragraphs.en:
Organizations often respond to uncertainty by asking for more data. Another survey, dashboard, model, expert opinion, or pilot can feel safer than deciding with incomplete information. But information is not automatically valuable. Its economic value depends on whether it can change the action and improve the expected outcome enough to justify the cost of obtaining it.

Consider a company deciding whether to enter a new market. Management believes demand could be high or low. If demand is high, entering creates substantial value. If demand is low, entering destroys value. The company can act now or run a market test first. The test matters only because its result may lead management to choose differently.

This is the core idea behind the value of information. First identify the best decision using current beliefs. Then imagine receiving new information and being allowed to choose again. If the new information would sometimes change the preferred action, it may have decision value.

A useful benchmark is perfect information. Suppose you could know the true future state before deciding. The improvement in expected outcome from that knowledge provides an upper bound on what any imperfect study should be worth. A real survey or model should not rationally cost more than perfect knowledge would save or earn.

This framework produces a surprising result: high uncertainty does not necessarily mean information is valuable. Imagine that demand could be either 1.5 million or 2 million units, but the project is profitable in both cases. You may be very uncertain about the exact number, yet the decision is the same: launch. Better forecasting may improve planning, but it does not change the launch decision itself.

The opposite is also true. Modest uncertainty can be highly valuable near a decision threshold. Suppose the investment is attractive only if expected demand exceeds one million units and the current estimate is close to that boundary. A relatively small improvement in knowledge may frequently switch the decision from “invest” to “do not invest,” or vice versa.

This is why analysts should begin with the decision, not with the available data. Ask what alternatives exist, what outcome matters, and what threshold changes the recommendation. Only then ask which unknowns are capable of moving the decision across that threshold.

Information quality also matters. Real evidence is noisy. Surveys contain response bias. Experiments may have limited samples. Models make classification errors. The relevant question is not whether the evidence is perfect, but how much it changes the probability of important states and whether that change is strong enough to alter action.

Timing can reduce information value. A six-month study may provide excellent evidence but arrive after a contract deadline or market window. Waiting may also impose opportunity cost. Therefore analysts should compare the benefit of learning with both the direct research cost and the cost of delay.

Sometimes waiting produces information naturally. A company may learn about demand from early customer inquiries, competitor moves, or regulatory decisions. If those signals will arrive soon, delaying an irreversible commitment can be valuable. But if delay allows competitors to lock up distribution or talent, waiting can destroy value.

Small pilots are powerful because they combine learning with limited commitment. A pilot can reveal adoption, implementation cost, failure modes, or customer behavior before the organization invests at full scale. Its value may come less from the pilot’s immediate profit than from the decisions it improves later.

The concept also helps prioritize analytical work. Suppose a team has five uncertain inputs in a business case. Improving the estimate of office expenses from plus or minus ten percent to plus or minus two percent may not change the decision. Improving the estimate of customer retention may change it dramatically. The second analysis has higher decision value even if the first is easier to measure precisely.

Value-of-information thinking can also prevent analysis paralysis. Teams sometimes continue collecting evidence simply because uncertainty remains. But complete certainty is usually impossible. A better stopping rule is to ask whether the remaining uncertainty is likely to change the action enough to justify another round of analysis.

This principle applies to AI and machine learning as well. A model with slightly better AUC may have little business value if both models produce the same operational decisions. Conversely, a modest improvement near a high-cost decision boundary may be extremely valuable if it changes which cases receive manual review or intervention.

The framework does not eliminate judgment. Probabilities, payoffs, and organizational constraints are themselves uncertain. Some decisions also involve ethics, regulation, or strategic commitments that cannot be reduced to one expected-value calculation.

Still, the discipline is useful. Before commissioning more research, define the decision and ask: What result would make us choose differently? How likely is that result? How much would choosing differently improve the outcome? What will the evidence cost, and what will we lose by waiting?

If no plausible result would change the action, the information may still be interesting, but its decision value is low. If several plausible results would change the action and the consequences are large, learning can be worth significant effort.

The most valuable information is therefore not necessarily the information that makes a forecast most precise. It is the information that helps an organization choose differently when choosing differently matters.
paragraphs.zh: 資訊的價值不在於讓預測更精準，而在於是否可能改變實際決策。應先定義 decision threshold，再判斷哪些未知能讓選擇跨過門檻，並比較研究成本、等待成本與改善決策的期望價值。
